title: Temperature Change by Elevation Calculator
description: Estimate how temperature changes with elevation using the Temperature Change by Elevation Calculator — the standard lapse rate, applied. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, on a standard-lapse day a 30°C (86°F) afternoon at sea level becomes about 19.5°C (67°F) up in Denver at 5,279 feet — the mile-high discount, computed.
quick_answer: The Temperature Change by Elevation Calculator estimates the temperature at a different elevation from a starting temperature, using the standard lapse rate of 6.5°C cooler per 1,000 metres climbed. Enter the starting temperature and the elevation change and read the estimate — for summit forecasts, pass crossings and packing decisions.

A valley holiday and a high-camp night are two climates on one trip. Estimating both ends stops the classic mistake of dressing for the car park.
Crossing a 2,000 m pass between two warm valleys means a midday stop near freezing in shoulder seasons — worth knowing before the convertible top goes down.
A forecast that shows the summit warmer than the standard estimate is not automatically wrong — inversions exist — but it has explaining to do.

examples.label: Example · Sea level to Pikes Peak

body.t: Pikes Peak rises 4,302 m. Standard lapse: 6.5 × 4.302 ≈ 28.0°C colder — a 30°C plains day becomes roughly 2°C at the summit, before wind has its say.
In imperial terms the standard rate is about 3.6°F per 1,000 feet. A 5,000-foot climb from an 80°F trailhead estimates to about 62°F — the version of the rule American hikers actually carry.

popular_table.title: Standard-lapse estimates
popular_table.intro: Computed at 6.5°C per 1,000 m from a 30°C (86°F) start — the estimator's own arithmetic.
popular_table.note: The standard lapse rate is an average atmosphere, not a promise. Dry air cools faster (up to about 9.8°C/km), saturated air slower (near 5°C/km), and inversions break the rule entirely.

faq: Why do mountains feel colder than the estimate?
Wind, exposure and radiation do what the lapse rate does not model. The estimate is the air's temperature; what you feel adds wind chill and sun, or the lack of it.
Does the estimate work going down?
Yes — descending air warms at the same standard rate in this model, which is why valleys and basins can be startlingly warm below a cool plateau.

On calm clear nights, cold air pools in valleys and temperature can rise with elevation — the reverse of the standard. The calculator models the standard atmosphere and says so; inversion mornings are the known exception.
Should I use this for aviation planning?
Only as background intuition. Flight planning uses forecast soundings and official meteorological data, not a single standard rate — density and icing decisions are not lapse-rate arithmetic.
How does humidity change the answer?
Rising saturated air cools more slowly (around 5°C/km) because condensing vapour releases heat. Humid ranges run warmer aloft than the standard suggests; deserts run colder.
Yes — the calculator handles °F inputs, applying the equivalent rate of about 3.6°F per 1,000 feet.
Why 6.5 and not some other number?

It is the International Standard Atmosphere's tropospheric lapse rate — a defined average chosen for engineering and aviation consistency, refined by this page's sibling tools when you have two real measurements.
